summary: Where things are: עַל “on”, מִתַּחַת לְ “under”, לְיַד “next to”, לִפְנֵי “in front of”, מֵאֲחוֹרֵי “behind”, בֵּין … לְ… “between … and …”, and בְּ “in” (בַּמְּקָרֵר). In the present there is no verb: הַסֵּפֶר עַל הַשֻּׁלְחָן “the book (is) on the table”. Several of them are built from body and space words: לִפְנֵי “to the face of”, לְיַד “at the hand of”, מִתַּחַת “from under”, מֵאֲחוֹרֵי “from the back of”. Two of them take a second preposition: מִתַּחַת לְ… and בֵּין X לְY. Near and far are adjectives that agree with their noun and take different prepositions: קָרוֹב לְ… “close to”, רָחוֹק מִ… “far from” (הַתַּחֲנָה קְרוֹבָה לַבַּיִת). Without a noun: בִּפְנִים “inside”, בַּחוּץ “outside”, מִשְּׂמֹאל “on the left”, מִיָּמִין “on the right” — and with movement the ending ־ָה: פְּנִימָה, הַחוּצָה, שְׂמֹאלָה, יָמִינָה. The noun after a preposition never changes (no cases): only the article fuses with לְ and בְּ (מִתַּחַת לַשֻּׁלְחָן, בַּמִּטְבָּח).

blocks.title: Thing — preposition — place
blocks.text: הַסֵּפֶר עַל הַשֻּׁלְחָן. The present needs no verb — not even one for “lies” or “stands”; in the past or future add הָיָה / יִהְיֶה (הַסֵּפֶר הָיָה עַל הַשֻּׁלְחָן).

blocks.title: מִתַּחַת needs לְ
blocks.text: מִתַּחַת לַשֻּׁלְחָן “under the table” — never *מִתַּחַת הַשֻּׁלְחָן. (Formal written Hebrew also has תַּחַת הַשֻּׁלְחָן, without לְ.)

blocks.title: Behind is not after
blocks.text: מֵאֲחוֹרֵי הַבַּיִת “behind the house”; אַחֲרֵי is “after” in time (אַחֲרֵי הָאֲרוּחָה).

blocks.title: לְ near, מִ far
blocks.text: קָרוֹב לַבַּיִת “close to the house” but רָחוֹק מֵהַבַּיִת “far from the house”.

blocks.title: לִפְנֵי is also “before” and “ago”
blocks.text: לִפְנֵי הַבַּיִת “in front of the house”, לִפְנֵי הָאֲרוּחָה “before the meal” (lesson 15), לִפְנֵי שָׁנָה “a year ago” — like German vor.

blocks.title: Ask yourself
questions: Where exactly: on, under, next to, in front of, behind, between, in?
Does it need a second preposition? (מִתַּחַת לְ, בֵּין … לְ)
Near or far? → קָרוֹב לְ… / רָחוֹק מִ…, agreeing with the noun.
No noun after it? → בִּפְנִים, בַּחוּץ, מִשְּׂמֹאל, מִיָּמִין.

askYourself: Which relation: on → עַל; under → מִתַּחַת לְ; next to → לְיַד; in front of → לִפְנֵי; behind → מֵאֲחוֹרֵי; between → בֵּין … לְ; in → בְּ.
Does the preposition need לְ after it (מִתַּחַת, בֵּין)? → add לְ and fuse it with the article: לַשֻּׁלְחָן.
Is it near or far? → קָרוֹב לְ… / רָחוֹק מִ…; make it agree: קְרוֹבָה, רְחוֹקִים …
Is there no noun after it? → בִּפְנִים / בַּחוּץ / מִשְּׂמֹאל / מִיָּמִין; with movement פְּנִימָה / הַחוּצָה / שְׂמֹאלָה / יָמִינָה.
Present tense? → no verb: הַסֵּפֶר עַל הַשֻּׁלְחָן.
Behind or after? → place מֵאֲחוֹרֵי, time אַחֲרֵי.
steps: Name the place; no verb in the present.

traps: קָרוֹב / רָחוֹק agree: הַתַּחֲנָה קְרוֹבָה, הַכְּפָרִים רְחוֹקִים.
“Close to” takes לְ, “far from” takes מִ.
לְיַד takes no לְ after it: לְיַד הַבַּיִת.
“On the left” is מִשְּׂמֹאל (where), “to the left” שְׂמֹאלָה (where to).

quiz.why: מִתַּחַת needs לְ, fused with the article: לַסַּפָּה. אַחֲרֵי means “after”.
מֵאֲחוֹרֵי is “behind”; אַחֲרֵי “after”; לִפְנֵי “in front of”.

quiz.q: הַתַּחֲנָה ___ לַבַּיִת. (The stop is close to the house.)
quiz.why: תַּחֲנָה is feminine singular, so קְרוֹבָה.
Far takes מִ “from”; near takes לְ “to”.
Location: מִשְּׂמֹאל; שְׂמֹאלָה is the direction “to the left”.
לִפְנֵי is “in front of”, “before” (time) and “ago” — like German vor.

seeAlso.note: Arabic عَلَى, تَحْتَ and بَيْنَ are the same words as Hebrew עַל, תַּחַת and בֵּין; Arabic puts the noun after them in the genitive.
German auf, unter, neben, vor, hinter, zwischen take the dative for “where” and the accusative for “where to”; Hebrew nouns never change, and “where to” uses other words (שְׂמֹאלָה, הַחוּצָה).
Chinese puts the place word after the noun (桌子上 “on the table”, 床下 “under the bed”) with 在 before it; Hebrew puts the preposition before the noun.

notes.text: Greek builds the same picture, often with two words: πάνω στο τραπέζι (עַל), κάτω από (מִתַּחַת לְ), δίπλα σε (לְיַד), μπροστά από (לִפְנֵי), πίσω από (מֵאֲחוֹרֵי), ανάμεσα σε (בֵּין). Like κοντά σε / μακριά από, Hebrew says קָרוֹב לְ / רָחוֹק מִ.
Russian на столе / под столом need cases, and often a posture verb (книга лежит на столе); Hebrew needs neither: הַסֵּפֶר עַל הַשֻּׁלְחָן.

encima de, debajo de, al lado de, delante de, detrás de, entre — Hebrew has one or two words for each (עַל, מִתַּחַת לְ, לְיַד, לִפְנֵי, מֵאֲחוֹרֵי, בֵּין … לְ), and no estar: הַסֵּפֶר עַל הַשֻּׁלְחָן.
“Close to / far from” are the same in Hebrew: קָרוֹב לְ / רָחוֹק מִ. But there is no “is” and no “lies / stands”: הַסֵּפֶר עַל הַשֻּׁלְחָן.
sur, sous, à côté de, devant, derrière, entre ~ עַל, מִתַּחַת לְ, לְיַד, לִפְנֵי, מֵאֲחוֹרֵי, בֵּין; près de / loin de ~ קָרוֹב לְ / רָחוֹק מִ — but Hebrew has no verb in the present.

German says where something is with a posture verb and the dative (Das Buch liegt auf dem Tisch) and where it goes with the accusative (auf den Tisch); Hebrew needs no verb and no case: הַסֵּפֶר עַל הַשֻּׁלְחָן.
Hindi uses postpositions after the noun (मेज़ पर, मेज़ के नीचे); Hebrew puts the preposition first: עַל הַשֻּׁלְחָן, מִתַּחַת לַשֻּׁלְחָן.
Persian also puts the place word first, often a noun with ezafe (روی میز “on the table”, literally “face of the table”) — just as Hebrew לִפְנֵי “in front of” comes from “face”.
Marathi puts the place word after the noun (टेबलावर “on the table”, टेबलाखाली “under the table”); Hebrew puts it first: עַל הַשֻּׁלְחָן.

Arabic عَلَى, تَحْتَ, بَيْنَ, أَمَامَ, وَرَاءَ come first too, and no verb is needed (الْكِتَابُ عَلَى الطَّاوِلَةِ ~ הַסֵּפֶר עַל הַשֻּׁלְחָן; עַל ~ عَلَى, בֵּין ~ بَيْنَ). Only Hebrew has no case after them.

Turkish says “the table’s top-on” (masanın üstünde); Hebrew puts the preposition first: עַל הַשֻּׁלְחָן. Turkish yakın / uzak take -e / -den (eve yakın, evden uzak) — the same “to / from” split as קָרוֹב לְ / רָחוֹק מִ.
Japanese says “the desk’s top-at” (机の上に) and needs ある / いる; Hebrew puts the place word first and needs no verb: עַל הַשֻּׁלְחָן.
Korean says 책상 위에 “desk top-at” and needs a verb of existence; Hebrew says עַל הַשֻּׁלְחָן with no verb in the present.
Finnish uses cases or postpositions (pöydällä, pöydän alla); Hebrew uses prepositions before the noun: עַל הַשֻּׁלְחָן, מִתַּחַת לַשֻּׁלְחָן.
Hungarian uses suffixes and postpositions (az asztalon, az asztal alatt); Hebrew uses prepositions before the noun.
Swahili juu ya, chini ya, karibu na, mbele ya, nyuma ya also come before the noun with a small linking word, much like Hebrew מִתַּחַת לְ….
Chinese wraps the place: 在 + noun + 上 / 下 / 旁边 (在桌子上); Hebrew uses one preposition before the noun: עַל הַשֻּׁלְחָן.
Vietnamese also puts the place word first (trên bàn, dưới bàn); Hebrew: עַל הַשֻּׁלְחָן, מִתַּחַת לַשֻּׁלְחָן.
Inuktitut says where something is with a location noun carrying a case ending, after the thing it relates to; Hebrew uses a preposition before the noun: עַל הַשֻּׁלְחָן.
